passage:
Monday. Francis needed a decision from Shankar and wrote it in four lines: "Please approve the hall booking by Wednesday. 42 guests, 18,500 rupees, Saturday 6 pm. Reply yes or no." He read it aloud once, cut a sentence and sent it.

Tuesday. Shankar replied in two minutes: "Yes. Book it." Francis booked the hall within the hour.

Thursday. For the caterer he wrote another message: the point first, dates and numbers, and one exact ask: "Please confirm 42 meals by Friday noon." Reading it aloud, he trimmed a third of the words. The caterer confirmed before lunch.

qa.q: What were the number of guests and the cost in Francis's Monday message?
qa.a: The message gave 42 guests and 18,500 rupees.

qa.q: How was Francis feeling when reading the message aloud and cutting a sentence?
qa.a: Francis felt cautious about wasting the reader's time and eager to be clear, so he trimmed the message until Shankar could act on it quickly.

qa.q: Which habits made the caterer reply so quickly?
qa.a: Putting the point first, giving dates and numbers, making one exact ask, and reading aloud to trim a third of the words.

qa.q: How might Shankar have found Francis's Monday message compared with a long one?
qa.a: Easy to answer, since Shankar replied within two minutes with a yes.

grounding: Shows a skilled writer stating the point first, giving dates and numbers, ending with one exact ask and trimming after reading aloud.

passage: Omkar, sit down for a minute. I'm Rehana, and I'm not scolding, just telling you what happened to me. In my second year I sent my manager a two-page note about a delayed shipment. It came back with one line: "What do you want me to do, and by when?" I was stung. That night I rewrote it. First line: "Please approve a replacement order by Friday." Then three short sentences with the numbers: 400 units, delayed since the third. I read it aloud in the empty office and cut a third. The manager approved it within ten minutes. Since then I write the point first, the numbers next and the exact action last.

qa.q: What was the one line the manager wrote back?
qa.a: The manager wrote: "What do you want me to do, and by when?"

qa.q: How did Rehana feel when the note came back with only one line?
qa.a: Stung and embarrassed, since the long note had not been read as hoped.

qa.q: What turning point that night changed the result?
qa.a: Rehana rewrote the note with the request in the first line, then dates and quantity, read it aloud and cut a third.

qa.q: Why might the manager have replied with only one line?
qa.a: The two-page note buried the request, so the manager needed to know what to do and by when, and the one line pointed at that missing part.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how a long note was returned and how a point-first, specific, trimmed rewrite got quick action.

passage:
Boarding closed in twelve minutes, and Rafiq still hadn't written the handover. He would be away for ten days. Chaitanya would run the vendor payments alone.
He sat on the floor near gate 22, laptop on his knees, and typed fast. Then he stopped, read it under his breath, and winced. Too long. He cut the part about why the old system was bad. He cut two "just to be safe" lines. He cut a third of it.
What he sent at 9:48:
"Chaitanya, three things while I'm away (12 to 21 March):
1. Pay Sharma Traders on 15 March, ₹48,000, invoice in the 'March' folder.
2. Do NOT pay Nair Supplies until they send the corrected invoice.
3. If the bank portal locks, call Mr Das on extension 98.
Action for you today: confirm you can see the March folder."
Chaitanya replied at 9:53: "Can see it. All clear. Safe flight 🙂"

qa.q: When should Sharma Traders be paid?
qa.a: Pay Sharma Traders on 15 March.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq wince after reading the draft under his breath?
qa.a: Rafiq felt uneasy because it was too long, and he was worried Chaitanya would miss what mattered.

qa.q: Which habits in Rafiq's note could anyone use?
qa.a: Putting the point first, giving exact dates and amounts, cutting a third after reading it aloud, and ending with the action needed today.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya feel reading the note?
qa.a: Chaitanya likely felt relieved and confident, replying within five minutes that it was all clear.

grounding: Illustrates a writer under time pressure who puts the point first, gives dates and numbers, cuts a third and ends with the exact action.

passage:
Anand, the new secretary of Laxmi Nagar Housing Society in Pune, had written his first notice about the water tank cleaning. It filled a whole page. It explained the history of the tank, a complaint from last year, the name of the cleaning company, and near the bottom, the actual dates.
He read it aloud to his neighbour Gautam over tea on the landing.
Gautam listened, then asked, "So when is there no water?"
Anand found the line. It was in the second-last paragraph. He laughed at himself.
They sat with a pencil. Anand read each sentence aloud; if Gautam didn't need it, it went. The page became six lines:
"No water: Saturday 14 June, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. (tank cleaning).
Please store water on Friday night.
Lift will run as usual.
Questions: Anand, Flat B-204."
He printed it and stuck it by the lift. On Saturday, not one resident knocked on his door to ask.

qa.q: Where did Anand stick the notice?
qa.a: He printed it and stuck it by the lift.

qa.q: How did Anand feel when Gautam asked when there was no water?
qa.a: Anand felt a bit embarrassed but amused, laughing at himself when he found the key line near the bottom.

qa.q: Which method turned the page into six lines, and why does it work?
qa.a: Reading each sentence aloud and cutting what the reader didn't need, because it shows the notice from the reader's side.

qa.q: How might the residents see the final notice?
qa.a: They would find it easy to act on, which is why nobody needed to knock and ask on Saturday.

grounding: Shows a writer who reads a notice aloud, cuts it hard and puts the date, time and action first.

passage:
"Samir, can you look at this before I send it to the director?" Shalini turned her screen.
Samir read for a moment. "What do you want her to do?"
"Approve two more interns for the summer."
"Where does it say that?"
Shalini scrolled. "Paragraph four."
"Put it first. Line one: 'Request: approval for two summer interns, June to August.'"
"Won't that sound rude?"
"It sounds clear. Then why, in two short sentences. Numbers, not adjectives."
"So not 'a heavy workload'?"
"'Three new clients, forty extra hours a week.' Then the exact action at the end."
"'Please approve by Friday so we can post the listing on Monday.'"
"Good. Now read the whole thing aloud."
Shalini read. Halfway through she stopped. "This paragraph about last year is… not needed."
"Cut it."
She cut it, and two more lines. "It's a third shorter."
"And twice as likely to get a yes," Samir said.

qa.q: How many summer interns is Shalini asking for?
qa.a: Approval for two summer interns, June to August.

qa.q: Why did Shalini worry about putting the request first?
qa.a: Shalini was worried it would sound rude to the director to start with the ask.

qa.q: What steps did Samir suggest to make the email better?
qa.a: Put the request first, give reasons with numbers in short sentences, end with the exact action and date, then read it aloud and cut.

qa.q: How might the director feel reading the shorter email?
qa.a: The director would likely feel it is easy to decide on, since the request, reason and deadline are clear in seconds.

grounding: Illustrates a writer who learns to state the point first, use short sentences with numbers, end with the exact action and cut a third by reading aloud.

passage: Last month I wrote the most useful email of my job so far, and it was also the shortest. I'm Raghav, and I handle supplies for our twelve bakery outlets. The flour supplier was changing on 1 March. My first draft opened with three paragraphs of background: the old supplier's delays, the tasting we'd done, my views on the new packaging. I read it aloud at my desk and got bored of my own voice halfway through. So I cut. The final version began: "From 1 March, flour comes from a new supplier. You need to do one thing." Then: "Deliveries arrive Tuesday and Friday before 7 a.m., not daily." Then: "Please send me your weekly flour quantity by 24 February." One short paragraph of background came last. The email shrank by about a third, and every line had a job. By the 24th, eleven outlets had replied. Gopika, my manager, forwarded it to the other region with one line: "Write like this."

qa.q: By what date did Raghav ask outlets to send their weekly flour quantity?
qa.a: By 24 February.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel reading the first draft aloud?
qa.a: Raghav felt bored by it, which was the signal to cut; afterwards Raghav seems quietly proud of the short version.

qa.q: Which changes made the final email work?
qa.a: The point came first, the sentences were short, the dates and days were exact, and it ended with one clear action and a deadline.

qa.q: How does Gopika see Raghav's email?
qa.a: Gopika sees it as a model and forwards it to the other region with "Write like this".

grounding: Illustrates a writer who puts the point first, uses short sentences with exact dates, ends with the action needed, and improves the draft by reading it aloud and cutting.
